This page describes the legacy Docker Compose stack — pvarki/docker-rasenmaeher-integration — which runs Deploy App in production today. Its successor is the Kubernetes platform described in Platform overview; if you are deciding which one to run, start with Choose your platform. Here you get the whole compose topology and service inventory on one page.

What the legacy stack is

docker-rasenmaeher-integration (codename RASENMAEHER) is an integration repo: it contains almost no application code itself. Each component — the core API, the UI, the CA, Keycloak, the product servers and their integration APIs — lives in its own repository and is pulled in as a git submodule. The top-level docker-compose.yml builds an image from each submodule directory and wires the containers together with shared volumes and Docker networks on a single host. A release of the stack is a tag of this repo, which pins a known-good combination of submodule commits (git checkout <TAG> + git submodule update --init --recursive).

Two properties shape everything else:

  • Field-deployment lifecycle. A deployment has a design lifetime of 1–2 months: the internal CFSSL CA defaults to CFSSL_CA_EXPIRY=2016h (12 weeks) and end-entity certificates to CFSSL_SIGN_DEFAULT_EXPIRY=1008h. Extending these is possible via env but explicitly not recommended by the README. docker compose down -v destroys the CA and every enrolled user.
  • Convergence by startup ordering, not by an orchestrator. There is no control plane; depends_on conditions (service_healthy, service_completed_successfully) plus an autoheal watchdog container stand in for what Kubernetes does with controllers and probes on the successor platform.

The Kubernetes port (pvarki/opendefence-platform, closed alpha) re-implements this same architecture with cert-manager instead of CFSSL, Traefik instead of nginx, and one CNPG database cluster per service instead of a shared Postgres container — each section below links its counterpart.

Service inventory

Everything below comes from the production docker-compose.yml. All pvarki/* images are published on ghcr.io and additionally carry a -d<RELEASE_TAG> suffix (default 2.9.0) tying the component build to the composition release; the suffix is omitted from the table for brevity.

Core and identity

The core is covered in depth in Core services & products (legacy); the Kubernetes equivalents are on Core services.

Service Image (default) Role
rmapi pvarki/rmapi:1.16.0-260523 The core REST API (rasenmaeher) on port 8000, internal only — user/enrollment management, cert issuance orchestration, product onboarding. Holds JWT signing keys in the rmapi_data volume.
rmui pvarki/rmui:2.3.1-260506-default One-shot: builds/delivers the static Deploy App UI into the rmui_files volume, which rmnginx serves. Not a running server in production.
keycloak pvarki/keycloak:24.0.5 Identity provider, realm RASENMAEHER. Serves its own TLS on port 9443 (published to the host) with --https-client-auth=request.
keycloak-init adorsys/keycloak-config-cli:6.1.6-24 One-shot: imports the realm configuration into Keycloak and wires LDAP federation (ldap://openldap:1389).
openldap pvarki/openldap:1.0.0 User directory backing Keycloak, root dc=example,dc=org. LDAPS on 1636 is published to the host.
postgres postgis/postgis:15-3.4 One shared PostgreSQL/PostGIS container. pg_init/ scripts create separate databases and users: keycloak, raesenmaeher, tak, battlelog, rmmtx, synapse.

PKI and provisioning

Detail on PKI: CFSSL & miniwerk (legacy); Kubernetes counterpart PKI & trust.

Service Image (default) Role
miniwerk pvarki/miniwerk:1.8.2-260524 One-shot that runs first: acquires Let's Encrypt server certificates (or mkcert fallback) into the le_certs volume, binding host port 80 for HTTP-01 while it runs, and writes per-product "kraftwerk" manifests into the kraftwerk_shared_* volumes. MW_PRODUCTS: "tak,kc,bl,mtx,matrix,synapse" drives the subdomain set.
cfssl pvarki/cfssl:api-1.2.0_260427 Internal CA signing API on port 8888; rmapi calls it to mint end-user client certificates. CA state lives in cfssl_data, the public chain in ca_public.
ocsp pvarki/cfssl:ocsp-1.2.0_260427 OCSP responder on port 8889, proxied publicly at https://<domain>/ca/ocsp. Unlike the Kubernetes alpha, the legacy stack has working OCSP end to end (TAK_OCSP_ENABLE: "true").
ocsprest pvarki/cfssl:ocsprest-1.0.7_260427 REST helper around CFSSL on port 8887, used by rmapi for revocation and CRL operations.

Edge (nginx)

Detail on Networking & subdomains (legacy); the Kubernetes stack replaces all of this with Traefik — see Ingress & network edge.

Service Image (default) Role
nginx_templates pvarki/nginx:templates One-shot: delivers the nginx config templates into the nginx_templates volume that both proxies render at startup.
rmnginx pvarki/nginx:1.31 The main public edge on :443. Serves the static UI from rmui_files and product UI bundles from ui_files, proxies /api to rmapi:8000, /ca/ocsp to the OCSP responder, and the Synapse upstream (synapse:8008). Terminates TLS (Let's Encrypt); on mtls.<domain> it also accepts client certificates (ssl_verify_client optional).
productsnginx pvarki/nginx:1.31 Consolidated proxy for product integration APIs on :4626 (client certificate required, ssl_verify_client on), plus :4627 for ephemeral ATAK auto-import downloads (ssl_verify_client off). Upstreams: takconfig:8003 (takrmapi shares that network namespace), rmmtx:8005, matrixrmapi:8012, blapi:3000, rmfpapi:8001.

Products and their integration APIs

Every product follows the same pattern — the product server plus a small *rmapi integration API that rasenmaeher talks to. The Kubernetes formalization of this pattern is described in Integration pattern.

Service Image (default) Role
takinit pvarki/takserver:5.7-RELEASE-32 One-shot (firstrun_rm.sh): initializes the TAK database and keystores.
takconfig / takmsg / takapi / takreten / takplug pvarki/takserver:5.7-RELEASE-32 TAK Server split into five JVM processes (config, messaging, API, retention, plugin manager). All except takconfig run with network_mode: "service:takconfig", so they share one network namespace; takconfig publishes 8089 (CoT/streaming), 8090-8094 (data feeds), 8443 (admin UI), 9000-9002 (federation).
takrmapi pvarki/takrmapi:1.13.0-260508-tak5.7-RELEASE-32 TAK integration API on port 8003, also inside the takconfig network namespace.
rmmtx pvarki/rmmtx:1.6.0-260513 MediaMTX integration/authz API on port 8005, with its rmmtx database in the shared Postgres.
mediamtx bluenviron/mediamtx:1.18.2 Streaming server. Publishes 1936 (RTMPS), 8322 (RTSPS), 8890/tcp+udp (SRT), 9888 (HLS), 9889 (WebRTC), 9996 (playback), 9997 (control API). Has no healthcheck — the container holds nothing but the mediamtx binary.
matrixrmapi pvarki/matrixrmapi:1.1.1-260512 Matrix integration API on port 8012; generates Synapse/OIDC configuration into synapse_config_vol.
synapse pvarki/synapse-dist:1.1.0-260507 Matrix homeserver on port 8008, proxied through rmnginx; database synapse in the shared Postgres.
blapi pvarki/blapi:1.1.0 Battlelog — API and UI in a single container on port 3000, database battlelog. The simplest product shape.

Utility containers

Service Image (default) Role
kwinit pvarki/kw_product_init:1.1.1 Build-and-exit: guarantees the kraftwerk init helper CLI image is built; product images use that Go binary to enroll with rasenmaeher.
kcinit pvarki/kc_client_init:1.0.0 Build-and-exit: same for the Keycloak OIDC client registration helper.
autoheal willfarrell/autoheal:latest Watchdog with /var/run/docker.sock mounted; restarts containers labeled autoheal=true when their healthcheck fails — a workaround for compose having no unhealthy-restart policy.
openldap_cert_perms, keycloak_cert_perms, mediamtx_cert_perms bash:latest One-shot chmod fixups so those services can read the Let's Encrypt certs in le_certs. Flagged FIXME in the compose file.

Honest note: several healthchecks are stubs — ocsp, openldap and all five TAK JVM services use test: 'true' (marked FIXME in the compose file), so autoheal cannot actually detect their failure.

blocks.html:
Three composition mechanisms hold this together:

Startup ordering. depends_on conditions enforce a strict bring-up chain: miniwerk (certs and manifests exist) and cfssl (the CA turns healthy) come up first, then postgres and openldap, then keycloak and its one-shot keycloak-init, then rmapi, then rmnginx (which also waits for the rmui and nginx_templates one-shots), and only then the products — each product tree waits for rmnginx to be healthy, and productsnginx starts last. TAK has its own internal chain: takinit → takconfig → takmsg → takapi, with takreten following takmsg and takplug/takrmapi following takapi.

Shared volumes as the integration fabric. There is no service discovery beyond Docker DNS; state and hand-offs travel through named volumes. ca_public (the CA chain) is mounted into nearly every container; le_certs carries the miniwerk-acquired server certificates to nginx, Keycloak, OpenLDAP, TAK and MediaMTX; kraftwerk_shared_<product> volumes hand each product its manifest (mounted at /pvarki), which the kw_product_init helper uses to enroll the product with rmapi — the volume-based ancestor of the Kubernetes ConfigMap wiring described in Integration pattern; ui_files collects product UI bundles for rmnginx to serve. Per-service data volumes (pg_data, cfssl_data, rmapi_data, tak_data, …) are the only persistence — the Kubernetes side's storage story is on Data & secrets.

Network segmentation. Eight Docker networks (apinet, kcnet, canet, ocspnet, dbnet, intranet, productnet, taknet) limit who can reach whom: only rmapi sits on six of them (it is the hub), the CA signing network canet holds just cfssl, ocsprest and rmapi, ocspnet extends to the proxies and takconfig (TAK performs live OCSP checks), and dbnet is shared by everything that owns a database. On Kubernetes this role is taken over by namespaces and the Linkerd mesh (Service mesh).

The submodule model

Every component is a pinned submodule; the integration repo turns them into images and the composition into a running host, as this build/composition flow shows.

blocks.html:
A stack release (RELEASE_TAG, currently defaulting to 2.9.0) stamps every locally-built image, so the images on a host can always be traced back to one tagged combination of submodules. Fourteen submodules are declared in .gitmodules; besides those in the diagram, kw_product_init, kc_client_init and fpintegration (the "fake product" reference integration, local/dev only) round out the set. The Kubernetes platform drops this model entirely — it consumes prebuilt ghcr.io/pvarki/* images pinned by tag in manifests, with no submodules (Deployment model).

Where things run

Everything runs on one Docker host — a single VM with DNS records for <domain> and the product subdomains (kc., tak., bl., mtx., matrix., synapse., plus their mtls. variants) pointing at it. Published host ports in production:

Port(s) Service Purpose
80 miniwerk HTTP-01 challenge, only while the one-shot runs
443 rmnginx UI, /api, OCSP proxy
9443 keycloak Keycloak's own TLS
1636 openldap LDAPS
4626 / 4627 productsnginx Product integration APIs / ephemeral ATAK downloads
8089, 8090-8094, 8443, 9000-9002 takconfig TAK streaming, data feeds, admin UI, federation
1936, 8322, 8890, 9888, 9889, 9996, 9997 mediamtx RTMPS, RTSPS, SRT, HLS, WebRTC, playback, control API

There are three composition files rather than compose profiles:

File Invocation What it is
docker-compose.yml docker compose up -d Production. Requires a .env with domain, CA name, LE email and all passwords.
docker-compose-local.yml rmlocal alias (-p rmlocal -f docker-compose-local.yml) Standalone full copy with development defaults: SERVER_DOMAIN=localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi, UI at :4439, baked-in passwords, plus the rmfpapi fake product.
docker-compose-dev.yml rmdev alias (layered on -local) Override file: devel_shell build targets, bind-mounted sources, rmapi under uvicorn --reload.

Resilience is deliberately minimal: restart: unless-stopped plus the autoheal watchdog, one non-replicated Postgres, and no backup tooling in the composition — the operational procedures live in Day 2 operations. On the Kubernetes platform the single host becomes a kind or k3s cluster with phased applies — see Deployment model. This page intentionally contains no install steps: those are owned by Deploy with Docker Compose.
